macro.ust_10y_basis: official close: Treasury daily par curve / Fed H.15, 2dp

US.why: Near horizons held, ten-year anchor held. Equities and bonds are telling different stories. The S&P closed at a record 7818.93 on 6 Oct (+0.58%), above its August high, the Nasdaq at a record 27599.79 (+0.45%) and the Dow at 51521.28 (+0.49%). The long end kept rising underneath them: on official closes the 10-year went from 5.17% on 25 Sep to 5.29% on 30 Sep and 5.31% on 5 Oct, after an intraday 5.349% that day, the highest since April 2002; the 30-year touched 5.69%, its highest since late May 2002. Growth is cooling at the edges - September payrolls added 29k against 84k, unemployment rose to 4.2%, consumer confidence fell to 81.9 and the ISM services index slipped to 54.9 - while services prices rose to 74.0. CME FedWatch had October at 21.6% and a December hike at 86.2% on 6 Oct. August core CPI was 2.4% y/y but +0.3% on the month, gasoline +27.4% y/y, and August PCE came in below forecast at 3.4%. Near horizons stay where the rate repricing put them: records on a 2002-high discount rate are a valuation risk, not a reason to restore them. The anchor holds at 6.5 on two structural points: the US is a net energy EXPORTER, a relative tailwind against every other bloc here, and NDX at 22.4x forward on its last verified reading sat below its 10y and 5y averages.
US.summary: Near horizons held: records on the S&P and Nasdaq with the 10-year at a 2002 high; the ten-year anchor holds at 6.5 on energy self-sufficiency.

EUROPE.why: The worst policy/growth mismatch in the world, and the inflation side keeps widening it. The ECB hiked to 2.50% on 10 Sep - its second and final move - into IMF growth of just 0.9% (the July update, up from 0.7%), and did it explicitly because the energy shock will hold inflation above target for an extended period. August HICP was 3.2% (final, from a 3.3% flash) with energy +14.3% y/y contributing 1.29 points of it. September's flash then jumped to 3.8%, above the 3.6% expected, with energy at 18.8%: the overshoot is the oil price, and it is growing. Europe is the largest net energy importer in the world facing Brent +55.87% y/y, and a final print at the flash on 16 Oct would test the ECB's word that its cycle is over. The offset is real - at 15.4x forward it is the cheapest large market here.
EUROPE.summary: Ranked last: the ECB hiked to 2.50% into growth of just 0.9%, and September's flash inflation jumped to 3.8% on 18.8% energy.

ASIA.why: Near horizons cut; Japan has run well past the September sell-off, Korea has not. The region sold off on 10-11 Sep - the Nikkei to 64,011 and KOSPI to 6,910 by the 11th, Samsung and SK Hynix leading the chip losses - and this time it is a rate shock as well as an energy one. The Nikkei closed at 69,946.86 on 5 Oct and 70,683.98 on 6 Oct, up 1.05% on the day, and the Tankan for large manufacturers rose to 24, an eight-year high. Korea was shut on 5 Oct and fell 0.89% to 6,941.39 on the 6th as foreigners sold Samsung (-1.45%) and SK Hynix (-3.69%) before their results. Saudi Aramco cut its November price to Asia to a six-year low - the first energy news in weeks that helps the region's importers - though China's halt to fuel exports keeps products tight. The BoJ delivered on 18 Sep, +25bp to 1.25% - the highest since 1995 - and the yen FELL, closing 156.86 per dollar, a two-week low. Read that carefully: a hike that weakens the currency is the market pricing the END of a cycle, not improving carry. The vote was 7-2, Asada and Sato dissenting, and August core CPI had slowed to 1.7% from 1.8% hours earlier, so the board tightened into decelerating headline inflation on the strength of a demand gauge at 1.9%. The gap from the previous move was three months against six before it: faster, and more contested. Korea, Taiwan and Japan are all large net oil importers. The ten-year anchor stays at 7.5: 10.5x forward against consensus EPS growth of ~52% and ~28% is a two-decade-wide discount, and JPM LTCMA puts EM equity at 7.8%, the highest of any equity block, on a framework that fits this mandate.
ASIA.summary: Ranked first over ten years: 10.5x forward against ~52% EPS growth; near horizons cut for a rate shock on top of an energy one.

PHILIPPINES.why: Near horizons cut, on the print this note named as the test. PSA put September inflation at 7.2% on 6 Oct, from 6.1%, inside BSP's 6.4%-7.4% range but above a 6.7% poll median, and core rose to 4.7% from 4.1%; food was 6.7%, transport 14.6%, and the poorest 30% of households saw 9.0%. The nominal carry is rising to meet it - the 5 Oct auction lifted 91-day bills to 5.667% and 364-day bills to 6.214%, up 9.9bp in a week - and BSP, at 5.00%, meets on 22 Oct with a larger hike now openly discussed. But against 7.2% every tenor's real yield is deeper below zero. The peso weakened to 62.771 on 6 Oct, 15 centavos on the day, against the weakest close on record of 62.86 on 14 Sep and the weakest intraday print of 62.925 the next day - a 6.34% loss of purchasing power against the dollar this year. The PSEi rebounded to 5743.21 on 5 Oct from its 2026 low of 5629.03 on 2 Oct, then fell 1.15% to 5677.12 on 6 Oct on the inflation print. Oil is easing - Brent settled at $100.58 on 6 Oct, +55.87% on a year earlier - but China's halt to fuel exports keeps imported products tight. The 12-month and ten-year horizons stay neutral: a BSP that hikes restores the real carry. This sleeve's job - zero duration risk and high nominal carry - is unimpaired. Its purchasing power is not.
PHILIPPINES.summary: Near horizons cut: September inflation hit 7.2% with core at 4.7%, pushing real T-bill yields further below zero before BSP meets on 22 Oct.

drivers.name: Monetary policy & liquidity
drivers.note: HELD at 2.0, the level the 3 Oct raise set - and the week tested it from both sides. October stayed off the table: CME FedWatch put it at 21.6% on 6 Oct, from 17% after the payrolls on 2 Oct and 73% on 23 Sep. But December firmed back to 86.2% on 6 Oct, from 66.2% on 2 Oct, and the long end made new highs. On official closes the 10-year went 5.12% on the 23rd, 5.18% on the 24th, 5.17% on the 25th, 5.24% on the 28th, 5.26% on the 29th, 5.29% on the 30th, 5.24% on the 1st, 5.28% on the 2nd and 5.31% on the 5th, after trading as high as 5.349% on 5 Oct, the highest since April 2002 (the 1 Oct peak of 5.342% is superseded). On 6 Oct it eased to about 5.27% on market quotes; no official close was found for that day. The 30-year touched 5.69% on 5 Oct, its highest since late May 2002, and read 5.659% on the 6th; the 2-year 4.80%. The trigger on the 5th was the ISM services report - activity cooler at 54.9, prices paid hotter at 74.0. Held rather than moved: the timing the 3 Oct raise was about has not reversed, and the level that held it to half has not improved. The ECB finished its own cycle on 10 Sep at 2.50%; BSP is at 5.00% after three hikes and meets on 22 Oct after a 7.2% CPI; the BoJ joined on 18 Sep at 1.25%. 16 of 18 dot-plot participants still saw one more hike this year.
drivers.summary: Held at 2.0: October hike odds are still low at 21.6%, but December firmed to 86.2% and the 10-year touched 5.349% on 5 Oct, a 2002 high.

drivers.name: Inflation trajectory
drivers.note: CUT a quarter point to 2.5 - the Philippine print this score was held for came in hot, and it was not alone. PSA put September inflation at 7.2% on 6 Oct, from 6.1%, above a 6.7% poll median and matching April's three-year high. Core jumped to 4.7% from 4.1%, the highest since October 2023, so it is not only oil and rice: food was 6.7% from 4.6%, transport 14.6% from 13.5%, and the poorest 30% of households saw 9.0%. US services prices are moving the same way: the ISM services prices index rose to 74.0 from 72.6 on 5 Oct. The euro-area flash for September was 3.8%, with energy at 18.8%. The US headline still eased - August PCE ran 3.4% and core 3.0%, against 3.7% and 3.3% expected, partly on the BEA's methodology change - and August core CPI was 2.4% y/y, +0.3% on the month against a 0.2% consensus, with gasoline +27.4% y/y and fuel oil +52%. Not cut further: oil is finally helping. Brent settled at $100.58 on 6 Oct, +55.87% on a year earlier, after Saudi Aramco cut its Asian price to a six-year low.
drivers.summary: Cut to 2.5: Philippine inflation jumped to 7.2% with core at 4.7%, US services prices hit 74.0 and the euro-area flash was 3.8%.

drivers.name: Growth momentum
drivers.note: HELD at 4.0 after the 3 Oct cut reversed the September raise. The new data are mixed rather than weak: the ISM services index was 54.9 in September, from 55.4 - a slight cooling, still well inside expansion - and manufacturing read 54.5. September payrolls added only 29k against 84k, unemployment rose to 4.2% and August was revised to +133k; consumer confidence fell to 81.9, the lowest since 2014. The S&P Global flash composite PMI was 58.4, the strongest since July 2021, and Japan's Tankan for large manufacturers rose to 24, an eight-year high. This driver's lane is whether the growth engine is intact under the shocks, not what the bond market does with the same print - that belongs to Monetary policy. The IMF's July update had already cut 2026 global growth to 3.0%, before the September rate shock took the 10-year to its highest since 2002.
drivers.summary: Held at 4.0: services cooled only slightly to 54.9 and manufacturing held 54.5, after 29k payrolls had reversed the September raise.

drivers.name: Corporate earnings
drivers.note: Still the strongest pillar. Asia ex-Japan EPS of ~+52% (2026) and ~+28% (2027) is unrevised. The chip trade is nervous before results rather than wrong: Samsung fell 1.45% and SK Hynix 3.69% on 6 Oct as foreigners sold ahead of earnings, after rising 2.79% and 3.21% on 2 Oct on Micron's results. Trimmed only for margins, and the margin picture is improving at the edge. Brent at $100.58 on 6 Oct is down from $105.28 on 28 Sep, and Saudi Aramco's Asian price cut makes crude cheaper for the region's manufacturers - though it is still far above the $64.53 of a year earlier. The estimates have not moved.
drivers.summary: Still the strongest pillar: Asia ex-Japan EPS of ~+52% this year; chips sold off before results on 6 Oct, Samsung -1.45% and SK Hynix -3.69%.

drivers.name: Valuation support
drivers.note: CUT a quarter point to 8.0, taking off the 23 Sep raise - as this note said one more week like the last would. The S&P closed at a record 7818.93 on 6 Oct, above its August high, and the Nasdaq at a record 27599.79, both with the 10-year at a 2002 high: the market re-rated through the rate shock instead of de-rating on it. That leaves the multiples reasonable rather than cheap. NDX at 22.4x forward on its last verified reading sat below its 10y (22.9x) and 5y (24.7x) averages; Asia at 10.5x is a two-decade-wide discount even with the Nikkei at 70,683.98; Europe is at 15.4x. A cheaper multiple on the same earnings is better compensation for the same risk, and this week the multiple got dearer.
drivers.summary: Cut to 8.0: the S&P and Nasdaq closed at records on 6 Oct, taking back the discount the 23 Sep raise was for.

drivers.name: Volatility & risk appetite
drivers.note: HELD at 3.0. The pairing with rates held again. The index rose 1.4% to 15.52 on 5 Oct as the 10-year made a new 2002 high, and fell 3.29% to 15.01 on 6 Oct as yields eased and stocks set records. The week before ran 16.07 on 28 Sep, 16.04, 16.34 and 16.39, then 15.31 on 2 Oct. It is still a low level - under the 17.84 close of 10 Sep and below the long-run 19.5 - so it reads as neither complacency nor stress. The curve is the 2 Oct strip (October 18.65 to January 20.38), five days old, which re-anchored to its own date reproduced the published VIX3M of 18.58 to within a quarter of a percent. What this driver does NOT carry is a claim that rising volatility pays the portfolio. Every fund's base return already assumes long-run volatility, so only the curve's distance from 19.5 moves a forecast. Blended across horizons the strip sits at 19.4 - just below it.
drivers.summary: Held at 3.0: the VIX fell 3.29% to 15.01 on 6 Oct as stocks set records; the curve blends to 19.4, just below its long-run 19.5.

drivers.name: Geopolitics & energy
drivers.note: HELD at 1.75 for a second week - the energy leg has normalised and the security leg has worsened, both as facts. Volume first, the measure this note says to read. Goldman's own series had Gulf oil exports, dark flows included, at 23.3 mb/d over the week to 29 Sep, in line with the 2025 average and above the 23.0 pre-war level implied by its 28 Aug note, which read 15.5. JPMorgan had Middle East crude at 17.5 mb/d, 98% of pre-war, though products only 58%. On 22 Sep Saudi Arabia restarted the 1200 km East-West (Petroline) pipeline, which had carried roughly 5.0 mb/d to Yanbu around the Strait; its energy minister put the flow at 5.8 mb/d on 6 Oct, from about 3.5 mb/d on 28 Sep. Producers are now competing for buyers: Saudi Aramco cut November Arab Light to Asia to $5 below the benchmark, from $2 below, a six-year low. The G7 plans a 100-million-barrel crude-and-diesel release, and the US offered the last 40 million barrels of its emergency release, leaving the reserve under 284 million barrels, the lowest since 1982. The price followed the barrels: Brent settled at $100.32 on 5 Oct and $100.58 on 6 Oct, from $102.25 on 2 Oct. Against that, the security facts. UKMTO logged nine attacks in the Strait in October by the 6th, half September's total of 18. On 5 Oct the IRGC turned a tanker back off Khasab under threat of attack. The queue off berth went back up to 242 vessels on 6 Oct, from 147 on 2 Oct, after a range that reached 443 on 22 Sep. Iran's president called talks with the US 'meaningless'; Qatar is working with China to restart them, and the President says the war will end around the 3 November midterms. Held, not raised: the barrels are flowing, but the ships carrying them are being hit at more than twice September's daily pace. Read the disruption on VOLUME, not vessel counts. The counts run from 1 to 30 a day depending on what is counted and when - IMF PortWatch 1 transit against an 85 baseline on its 27 Sep reading, Lloyd's List Intelligence 14 a day in the week to 23 Aug counting only cargo over 10000 dwt, the US government around 30 on a basis it does not state - and none of them is supply. Still close to the floor of 1: the Strait is shut to anything the US Navy does not escort, and the stress table's full closure with Brent above $130 is a strictly worse state still on the table.
drivers.summary: Held at 1.75: pipeline flows hit 5.8 mb/d and Brent fell to $100.58, but UKMTO logged nine Strait attacks in October's first six days.

funds.name: ATRAM Peso Money Market Fund
funds.target: Own mandate: outperform PH bank deposits, average portfolio duration <= 1 year
funds.gross_note: 10y average PH short-rate path. Anchored on the PH bill curve - 91d 5.667%, 182d 5.971%, 364d 6.214% at the 5 Oct auction, higher across the curve than when this assumption was set on 2 Sep - with BSP at 5.00% after a third consecutive hike, reverting toward a ~4.50% neutral policy rate by year 3-5. Held at 4.85% and flagged rather than re-fitted: the rise sits in the part of the path that reverts within a few years, which lifts a ten-year average by roughly a tenth of a point - inside this assumption's precision, but a known upward bias until it is re-fitted. CUT from 5.25% when the mandate lengthened to 10 years: the elevated front end is a 1-3 year feature, so over a decade far more of the path sits at neutral and the average falls toward it.
funds.dd_k_why: Not applicable - the cash sleeve is floored by a rate shock, not by the equity formula.

catalysts.why: The first read on how many of the 16 of 18 dot-plot participants who saw one more hike want it soon. October is priced at 21.6% and a December hike at 86.2% (FedWatch, 6 Oct); the minutes decide which of those moves.
The flash said 3.8%, from 3.2%, with energy at 18.8% - above the 3.6% expected. A final at or above it tests the ECB's word that its cycle ended at 2.50% on 10 Sep, and the Europe ranking with it.

BSP is at 5.00% after three hikes, the last on 27 Aug. September inflation printed 7.2%, core 4.7%: a hike lifts the peso sleeve's carry toward a positive real yield, a pause leaves it deeper below zero.

FedWatch has October at 21.6% and a hike by December at 86.2% (6 Oct), after 29k September payrolls took October off the table on 2 Oct. The dot-plot median has one more this year, so the question is when.

The date both sides of the Hormuz talks are working to. Iranian officials have said a deal is unlikely before it; the President says the war will end around it, and has called renewed strikes after it 'possible'. The stress table's full closure is the state this date can bring back.

postponed.what: Iran-GCC talks on the Strait, in Oman
postponed.why: Called off on 14 September with no new date; Iran was to unveil the temporary shipping lane agreed with Muscat. US and Iranian delegations met at the UN on 22 September instead, and that meeting is what restored the energy driver.

dd_model.note: 1.65 is the calibration anchor, not the coefficient every sleeve uses. Each fund carries a declared adjustment for the shape of its own left tail; the portfolio coefficient is the weighted average across the equity sleeves. The whole quantity is then scaled by sqrt(horizon / calibration window), because expected maximum drawdown grows with the square root of the horizon - the -20% and -33% anchors are rolling FIVE-year medians and cannot simply be relabelled for a longer mandate.
